editorialPurpose: In the triplewart seadevil, a male can permanently join a female through fused tissue and vascular connections, gaining nutrition while retaining his reproductive role; reproductive assurance is an evolutionary explanation.
storyAngle: Follow a pair through grip, tissue union and nutrition, then distinguish observed fusion from the proposed evolutionary advantage.

segments.text: Some fish physically fuse with their mates.
In the deep sea, a tiny male searches for a much larger female.
He grips her skin with hooked teeth. In this species, attachment becomes permanent.
Over time, their tissues join. Blood vessels connect.
Her blood supplies his nutrients, while his testes develop to produce sperm.
He doesn't disappear into her. He remains an attached male.
How can foreign tissues coexist? These fish have lost key parts of adaptive immunity.
Exactly how their remaining defenses work is still being studied.
In a world where mates are hard to find, staying together may secure future spawning.

narrativeStructure.label: A permanent encounter
narrativeStructure.purpose: Large female occupies frame with tiny male beside her ventral flank; short lure,3 dorsal caruncles and jaw establish species. Camera closes immediately; no empty water opening.

narrativeStructure.label: Search the water column
narrativeStructure.purpose: Track a large-eyed, lureless male swimming through black water; restrained distant point of female light and huge female silhouette emerge. Search direction is illustrative, not a proven tracking path.

narrativeStructure.label: Meet the triplewart
narrativeStructure.purpose: Reveal entire same female at near-profile angle; three dorsal caruncles, tiny female eye, small pectoral and short esca remain visible. Scientific species label.

narrativeStructure.label: Grip then remain
narrativeStructure.purpose: Continuous close-in approach ending with both jaw tips physically against female ventral skin; tiny hooked denticles visible only in macro. Hold the grip, no immediate vascular join.

narrativeStructure.label: Tissue then circulation
narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera enters the contact seam. Two adjoining tissue surfaces become continuous across a narrow junction; vascular lumen connection develops only later. Organic connected tissue, not floating cell grid.

narrativeStructure.label: Nutrition and reproduction
narrativeStructure.purpose: Follow illustrative paired vessel paths across the same narrow seam and into the recognizable male. Warm flow motion means nutrient transport only. Male remains whole; no detailed internal organ map or sperm-in-blood imagery.

narrativeStructure.label: Still two fish
narrativeStructure.purpose: Pull out from seam to show male retained externally, with body and fin movement; no shrinking into organ or disappearance.

narrativeStructure.label: Tolerance puzzle
narrativeStructure.purpose: Macro seam remains anatomically joined; secondary restrained visual distinction between intact tissue and absent rejection attack, no literal immune cells being switched off. Large adaptive-immunity label plus evolved-gene-loss qualification.

narrativeStructure.label: Defense remains open
narrativeStructure.purpose: Camera orbits joined tissue toward exterior. Both fish remain distinct. Research qualification legible; no pathogens, shields or speculative defense pathways.

narrativeStructure.label: Future spawning association
narrativeStructure.purpose: Return to matched opening view of attached pair in huge dark water column; camera widens while pair stays physically connected. No egg or sperm release not directly verified for species.

narrativeStructure.label: A lasting connection
narrativeStructure.purpose: Final gentle orbit of joined pair, female moves and male follows at exact attachment point; resolve first image with lasting physical association, no single-individual or love metaphor.
